items.title: Louis Armstrong: Jazz Casual Interview, 1964-07-10
items.q: the first record you made back with King Oliver in Chicago in 1923

ctx.x: Song Song This is Jazz Casual, I'm Ralph Gleason, and that voice and that music is the voice and

music of jazz as number one ambassador to the world, Louis Armstrong, who is with us today to talk about some of his music. Louis, welcome to Jazz Casual. Thank you very much. It's an honor to have you here, and I'm sure that, like many other people that have been interested in jazz, have been fans of jazz, I can say that I grew up loving this music, and this means that I grew up loving you, and been fascinated by it, and fascinated by the things you've done, and I've wanted to know so many different things about…

items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1961-02-10
items.q: And I just grew right up on the Joe. ... I used to run errands for King Oliver.

ctx.x: And put you in the waif's home, huh?

Yeah. So, now, he treated me nice there. The first thing they gave me was a big plate of beans, you know. And I was playing hard to get for two days, you know. But after that third day, I could see that big plate of beans walking down a long table, you know, at the last supper. Anyway, when I got used to the beans, and they come as to showing me how to blow the bugle, and I was the official bugle of the institution. Yeah. They couldn't drill. They couldn't eat. They couldn't do nothing. They had to go to bed by…
You know, New Orleans is one of the most picturesque cities in America. You spent your childhood there. When you think back about New Orleans, do you ever want to, what comes through your mind?

items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1962-09-19
items.q: I've always been a disciple to Joe Oliver... King Oliver taught me how to read music and everything.

ctx.x: Now, can you tell us, just how did you learn to blow that horn right now?

Well, I've always been a disciple to Joe Oliver, who was top man when I was a kid. And in the meantime, I used to go around the streets in a little quartet singing, and we'd pass the hat. And I don't know, there was celebration there around New Year's Eve, everybody shoot the big pistols and everything. And my mother kept on trying to hide my stepfather's pistol, but I found it. And I was shooting on Ramport Street, the big street in New Orleans, and the detective hugged me, and I cried like a little baby. But…
Now, Mr. Armstrong, around about 1930, I remember reading in the paper that you were dead.
